/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/related_work.tex:49:\citet{truong2025entropy} connects entropy collapse to critical transitions, characterizing it as a first-order phase transition with universality classes that determine whether classical early-warning signals retain predictive power.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/related_work.tex:64:\citet{yi2026causalcompass} benchmark causal discovery robustness under eight misspecification scenarios and confirm that no single method dominates universally, directly supporting the multi-method rationale of our consensus framework.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/related_work.tex:72:Our work applies this multiverse perspective to model collapse: five statistical methods across six contamination regimes produce conclusions that range from universal significance to complete null on the same dataset.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:66:For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:72:After correcting the statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$; however, the qualitative finding that this single hyperparameter can swing conclusions between near-universal significance and near-universal non-significance remains, consistent with known properties of the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical}.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:77:[Omitted long matching line]
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:268:This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:340:We note that bootstrap power${=}1.0$ reflects the effect size in our 4-seed data and should not be interpreted as a universal power guarantee; furthermore, the two methods use different data-generating processes for calibration (permutation Granger resamples observed $\alpha{=}1.0$ trajectories, while Toda--Yamamoto power was estimated under a generic VAR(2) simulation with $\beta{=}0.3$).
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:438:This domain-dependent directionality suggests that the unidirectional forward causation observed in WikiText may partly reflect domain-specific dynamics rather than a universal property of collapse; implications are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/experiments.tex:446:This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal across all architectures, enriching Claim~3 by adding canary metric selection as a further source of analytic variability.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/discussion.tex:74:The unidirectional forward causation observed consistently in WikiText experiments (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all contamination levels and seeds) does not hold universally.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/discussion.tex:87:This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/discussion.tex:161:[Omitted long matching line]
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/method.tex:22:At $\alpha{=}1.0$, canary$\to$perplexity pairs appear near-universally significant in undifferenced analysis ($F{=}16$--$36$) but yield $F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a; \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/method.tex:345:The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (\S\ref{sec:regime}) is consistent with the two universality classes of \citet{truong2025entropy}: if the transition is first-order (Class~1, irreversible, exponent $\nu{=}1$), the abrupt simultaneous shift in canary and downstream metrics suppresses the temporal lead that Granger tests exploit, while smoother second-order dynamics (Class~2, reversible, $\nu{=}1/2$) at neighboring $\alpha$ values preserve it.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/introduction.tex:15:In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_4/projects/distrib_canary_collapse/docs/paper/introduction.tex:33:To our knowledge, this constitutes the first multiverse-style analysis of lead-lag claims in model collapse: the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions that span the full spectrum from universal significance to complete null.

[Director 指令] [Patch — D129 核心理论] Per-Generation Signal Threshold 段落

## 插入位置
Section 3 (method.tex) 理论动机 subsection，在 "Four predicted detectability intervals" 段落之后，新增段落 "Detection threshold vs.\ accumulated contamination"。

## 内容

**核心数字**（必须出现在论文中）：
- α=0.45, generation 10: cumulative contamination = 1 - (1-0.45)^10 = 99.75%
- α=0.50, generation 10: cumulative contamination = 1 - (1-0.50)^10 = 99.90%
- Difference: 0.15 percentage points
- PermG: 0/8 → 6/8

**论证**：
Detection threshold depends on **per-generation mixing ratio α**, not cumulative contamination. This is because PermG detects inter-generation temporal lead-lag: the entropy shift at each generation is proportional to α × quality_gap(g), where quality_gap(g) captures the distributional distance between model-generated and real text at generation g. The critical threshold α_c ≈ 0.50 corresponds to the per-generation signal-to-noise ratio crossing the detection floor.

This distinction matters because prior work in data poisoning implicitly assumes that detection difficulty scales with total contamination. Our results show the opposite: two training runs with nearly identical cumulative contamination (99.75% vs 99.90%) produce categorically different detection outcomes (0/8 vs 6/8 significant pairs). The detection phase transition is governed by the intensity of each contamination episode, not the aggregate exposure.

**数学符号**：
- Per-generation signal: Δh(g) = H(p_g^{mixed}) - H(p_g^{clean}) ∝ α · d_TV(p_g^{model}, p^{real})
- Cumulative contamination: C(α, G) = 1 - (1-α)^G
- Detection depends on {Δh(g)}_{g=1}^G (the time series of per-generation shifts), NOT on C(α, G)

**写作要求**：
- 这段约 150-200 words
- 语气：semi-quantitative argument（不是 formal theorem）
- 先写 observation（0.15pp → 0/8 vs 6/8），再写 explanation（per-generation SNR），最后写 implication（overturns assumption）
- 这是 D129 Direction 1 "Detection ≠ Contamination" 的数学基础

These four regimes align with the empirical dose-response (\S\ref{sec:regime}): blind at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ (PermG 0/8), onset at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, dual-seed), synchronous dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (0--3/8, dual-seed), and detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ (5--6/8 per seed, three seeds; 6/8 per seed at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).
The non-monotonic profile is a prediction of the $S \times R$ framework, not an anomaly requiring post-hoc explanation; indeed, non-monotonic dose-response curves are well-documented across disciplines.
The four-regime profile mirrors the hormetic dose-response in toxicology, where intermediate doses produce qualitatively different effects from both low and high doses~\cite{calabrese2003hormesis}.
The temporal resolution collapse at intermediate $\alpha$ ($R \to 0$) corresponds to the known failure of Granger-type tests under contemporaneous coupling~\cite{deshpande2010instantaneous}: when entropy and diversity shift within the same generation (lag${=}0$), the causal test loses statistical power by construction, not by methodological deficiency.
The detection dip is also consistent with critical speeding-up phenomena in ecological regime shifts, where early-warning indicators exhibit non-monotonic behavior near phase boundaries rather than the monotonic rise predicted by classical critical slowing down~\cite{titus2020speeding}.
We emphasize that the $S \times R$ model provides qualitative intuition, not quantitative derivation; the regime boundaries depend on model capacity, dataset properties, and sample size $N$.

\paragraph{Connection to effective rank and detection layers.}
The link between entropy and diversity can be made more concrete through effective rank~\cite{roy2007effective}: $\mathrm{erank}(P) = \exp(H(P / \|P\|_1))$ measures the number of dimensions carrying substantial probability mass.
A decline in $H$ contracts $\mathrm{erank}(P)$, pushing tail tokens below $\tau_n$ and eliminating the $n$-grams they participate in.
This yields a mechanistic chain---$H$ decreases $\to$ $\mathrm{erank}$ contracts $\to$ tail probabilities cross $\tau_n$ $\to$ $D_k^{(g)}$ drops---in which entropy responds first.
This chain mediates the temporal resolution factor $R(\alpha)$: at intermediate $\alpha$ (${\approx}0.60$), relaxation time matching compresses the erank-mediated cascade into a single generation ($R \to 0$); at higher $\alpha$, the severity of entropy collapse outpaces the cascade, restoring the generational offset ($R$ large; \S\ref{sec:regime}).

Effective rank is a \emph{distributional dimensionality} indicator---it detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom---and is conceptually distinct from the classical critical slowing down (CSD) indicators (rising autocorrelation and variance) that characterize dynamical stability near tipping points~\cite{scheffer2009early,dakos2012methods}.
These two layers, together with the causal coupling layer captured by Granger-type tests, form complementary detection channels rather than redundant measures of the same phenomenon.

44	\paragraph{Three-layer detection taxonomy.}
45	Our results suggest a layered taxonomy for detecting iterative training degradation, ordered by onset threshold:
46	(1)~\emph{Distributional dimensionality} (effective rank): detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom, with onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.10$;
47	(2)~\emph{Causal coupling} (Granger-type tests): detects temporal precedence between canary and downstream metrics, with onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ (the detection phase transition established in \S\ref{sec:regime}); and
48	(3)~\emph{Dynamical stability} (classical CSD indicators: AC1, variance): theoretically predicted to detect rising autocorrelation near tipping points~\cite{scheffer2009early}, but untested at our sequence length ($T{=}11$; \S\ref{sec:limitations}).
49	These three layers are complementary rather than redundant: dimensionality collapse precedes causal detectability by a wide margin ($\alpha{\approx}0.10$ vs.\ $\alpha{\approx}0.50$), and the layers can diverge across architectures.
50	
51	\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
52	As a distributional dimensionality indicator, effective rank tracks contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom---Layer~1 in the taxonomy above.
53	However, effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
54	In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
55	In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
56	The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
57	This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines---a limitation specific to the dimensionality layer that does not affect the causal coupling layer (Granger detectability), which remains consistent across architectures.
58	
59	\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
60	Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
61	Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
62	This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method analysis: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.
63	
64	\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}
65	The non-monotonic dose-response at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (PermG fwd: s42 3/8, s43 0/8, below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $\alpha{=}0.75$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) is consistent with the $S \times R$ prediction in \S\ref{sec:theory}: at $\alpha{=}0.60$, relaxation time matching drives temporal resolution $R \to 0$---entropy and diversity respond within the same generation---so that despite increasing signal strength $S$, the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
66	At lower contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $R$ remains high---entropy leads diversity by a full generation---and $S$ has just crossed the detection threshold, yielding sufficient $S \times R$.
67	At higher contamination ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), $S$ grows large enough to dominate: entropy collapses within generation~0$\to$1 while diversity still requires generation~1$\to$2, restoring $R$ and driving $S \times R$ well above the detection floor.
68	The synchronous dip is mechanistically distinct from the blind regime: in the blind regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$), canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous dip, both metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

\paragraph{Three-layer detection taxonomy.}
Our results suggest a layered taxonomy for detecting iterative training degradation, ordered by onset threshold:
(1)~\emph{Distributional dimensionality} (effective rank): detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom, with onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.10$;
(2)~\emph{Causal coupling} (Granger-type tests): detects temporal precedence between canary and downstream metrics, with onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ (the detection phase transition established in \S\ref{sec:regime}); and
(3)~\emph{Dynamical stability} (classical CSD indicators: AC1, variance): theoretically predicted to detect rising autocorrelation near tipping points~\cite{scheffer2009early}, but untested at our sequence length ($T{=}11$; \S\ref{sec:limitations}).
These three layers are complementary rather than redundant: dimensionality collapse precedes causal detectability by a wide margin ($\alpha{\approx}0.10$ vs.\ $\alpha{\approx}0.50$), and the layers can diverge across architectures.

\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
As a distributional dimensionality indicator, effective rank tracks contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom---Layer~1 in the taxonomy above.
However, effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines---a limitation specific to the dimensionality layer that does not affect the causal coupling layer (Granger detectability), which remains consistent across architectures.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method analysis: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}
The non-monotonic dose-response at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (PermG fwd: s42 3/8, s43 0/8, below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $\alpha{=}0.75$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) is consistent with the $S \times R$ prediction in \S\ref{sec:theory}: at $\alpha{=}0.60$, relaxation time matching drives temporal resolution $R \to 0$---entropy and diversity respond within the same generation---so that despite increasing signal strength $S$, the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
At lower contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $R$ remains high---entropy leads diversity by a full generation---and $S$ has just crossed the detection threshold, yielding sufficient $S \times R$.
At higher contamination ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), $S$ grows large enough to dominate: entropy collapses within generation~0$\to$1 while diversity still requires generation~1$\to$2, restoring $R$ and driving $S \times R$ well above the detection floor.
The synchronous dip is mechanistically distinct from the blind regime: in the blind regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$), canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous dip, both metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

[Director 指令] [Reframe — D130] 论文从 Methodology Paper 转型为 Detection Phase Transition Discovery Paper

投稿目标：EMNLP 2026 ARR June cycle，8 页 main text + unlimited references + appendix。当前 37 页需大幅压缩。

## 核心叙事转变

**旧**："Method Matters" — 比较 5 种方法的 methodology paper → Findings 水平
**新**："Detection Phase Transition Discovery" — 发现 α_c≈0.50 的 detection phase transition → Accept 水平

Multi-method 分析从"贡献"降级为"发现工具"。Phase transition 从"结果之一"升级为"核心发现"。

## 4 个贡献（按重要性排序）

**C1: Detection Phase Transition**（核心发现）
- α_c=0.476 sigmoid onset (R²=0.969, k≥200, Δα≈0.02)
- Robust across 6 model families (Pythia 410M/1.4B/6.9B, GPT-2m, OPT-1.3B, Qwen-0.8B)
- **关键新发现**：Detection threshold = per-generation mixing ratio α, NOT cumulative contamination (99.75% vs 99.90% → PermG 0/8 vs 6/8)
- Null FPR: PermG 0/24 across 3 seeds

**C2: Theoretical Framework**（机制解释）
- S(α) × R(α) 竞争模型 → 预测非单调 5-regime dose-response
- Per-generation signal threshold: Δh(g) ∝ α · d_TV
- Predicts 5 regimes: blind → onset → sync dip → recovery → saturation
- Cross-disciplinary connections: Deshpande (2010) zero-lag GC failure, Calabrese (2003) hormesis, Titus (2020) critical speeding up

**C3: Multi-Method Diagnostic Toolkit**（方法贡献）
- 5 methods × 3 known pitfalls (FPR, direction, power)
- PermG = only zero-FPR method (0/24 vs diff 37.5%, threshold 25%)
- MMCT framework: K≥3 consensus 压缩个体 FPR
- 降级为"用什么工具发现的"，不是"发现了什么"

**C4: Practical Applications**（实践贡献）
- Four-layer detection taxonomy (dimensionality α≥0.10 / variance α≥0.25 / causal α≥0.50 / dynamical α≥0.50)
- Early cessation intervention: 15% entropy drop threshold, zero false alarm
- Data strategy warning: accumulate mode = collapse blind (PermG 0/8 vs replace 6/8, dual-seed)
- bf16 precision kills causal signal (0/8 vs fp32 6/8)

## 页面预算（8 页 main text）

| Section | Pages | Content |
|---------|-------|---------|
| Abstract + Intro | 1.5 | Phase transition discovery story, 4 contributions |
| Background + Related Work | 1.0 | Model collapse literature, Granger causality, phase transition theory |
| Theory + Method | 2.0 | S×R framework, 5-regime prediction, per-generation threshold, PermG/MMCT description |
| Results | 2.5 | Phase transition (sigmoid fit) + cross-arch + dose-response + cessation + data strategy |
| Discussion + Conclusion | 1.0 | Four-layer taxonomy, CSD suggestive evidence, limitations, future work |
| References | ~1 | |

**移到 Appendix**：MMCT 数学细节、完整 Table 7（所有 model×seed 组合）、per-method dose-response 细分图、null FPR 详细表、bf16 精度分析

## 标题建议
主选："A Detection Phase Transition in Iterative Training Collapse"
备选："Sharp Onset of Causal Detectability in Model Collapse" 或 "Method Matters" 作为 subtitle

## 写作约束
- 8 页硬限（EMNLP 2026 规则）
- "sharp onset" / "near-discontinuous onset"，不用 "first-order phase transition"
- "robust across architectures"，不用 "universal"
- CSD evidence = "suggestive"，不是 "confirmed"
- 所有引用需要验证
- Gu 2025 datamixing = NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight（不是 ICLR）

## 执行模式
这是 **Reframe**——需要重写 Abstract, Introduction, 重组 Results section, 压缩全文。不是增量 Patch。请生成 writing_plan.yaml 提交我审批。

\begin{abstract}
We show that lead-lag conclusions in iterative model collapse are fragile: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\% (inter-method $\kappa{=}0.091$--$0.185$), with the most liberal method yielding 75\% forward-direction FPR even at the null ($\alpha{=}0.0$).
We identify three pitfalls (method sensitivity, spurious regression under shared trends, and regime dependence) and systematically compare five statistical methods through a Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).
Permutation Granger causality emerges as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with high sensitivity, exhibiting a detection phase transition ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): 0/8 through $\alpha{=}0.45$, near-discontinuous onset at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, dual-seed), a non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (synchronous collapse), and reliable detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$ metric pairs) in 12 cases (86\%), with directional asymmetry (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) confirmed across four seeds on WikiText-103.
First-differencing cleanly separates genuine from spurious channels: all canary$\to$diversity leads survive while all canary$\to$perplexity leads vanish.
Applied to Pythia-410M and replicated across six model families (345M--6.9B parameters), the framework identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse, with canary-based predictive cessation validated across two model scales (410M, 1.4B).
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Several limitations constrain the generalizability of our findings.

\paragraph{Model scale.}
Our experiments are validated at scales ${\leq}1.4$B parameters (GPT-2-medium 345M, Pythia-410M, OPT-1.3B), all decoder-only transformers small by contemporary standards.
Whether the temporal lead shortens or vanishes at frontier scale (7B+) is an open question requiring proportionally more compute per condition: 10 generations $\times$ 5{,}000 steps per generation makes iterative training at 7B+ prohibitively expensive for academic settings.
Encoder-decoder architectures (T5, BART) and non-autoregressive models (e.g., diffusion-based text generators) are entirely untested; their fundamentally different generation mechanisms may alter canary dynamics in ways that autoregressive decoder-only results cannot predict.
The batch size difference between architectures (4 for Pythia vs.\ 32 for GPT-2-medium) means each training step exposes $8\times$ more data in the latter, potentially accelerating collapse dynamics without altering the qualitative pattern.

\paragraph{Data domain and scale.}
Training data is drawn from a 5K-document subset of WikiText-103, three orders of magnitude smaller than typical pre-training corpora.
This scale gap means our iterative training dynamics reflect a low-data regime where overfitting to synthetic content may onset faster than in production-scale pipelines.
Domain-specific properties (vocabulary richness, syntactic complexity, topical diversity) may further influence canary-downstream coupling, and domains with inherently low diversity (e.g., legal text, code) could exhibit different canary dynamics.
The C4-domain generalization experiments (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) introduce an additional confound: switching from WikiText to C4 simultaneously changes both the textual domain and the data-scale characteristics, preventing full disentanglement of domain effects from scale effects within a single experimental comparison.

\paragraph{Pre-training data confound (C4).}
Our C4-domain generalization experiments (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) use Pythia models that were pre-trained on the Pile~\cite{gao2021pile}, which includes Common Crawl data overlapping with C4.
This means the model has prior exposure to the domain used for iterative training, potentially conflating domain familiarity with collapse dynamics.
The WikiText-103 experiments do not share this confound because Pythia's pre-training corpus does not include WikiText-103 directly.
Interpreting C4 results therefore requires caution: observed differences from the WikiText baseline may reflect domain familiarity effects rather than genuine domain-dependent collapse behavior.

\paragraph{Short time series ($T{=}10$).}
With 11 data points per series, our statistical analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This limits power for all methods and renders two of the five evaluated methods effectively inoperative: threshold onset detection yields 0/8 significant pairs in the majority of conditions under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power relative to the primary methods (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Both threshold onset and Toda--Yamamoto are classified as supplementary: the former due to power limitations (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}), the latter due to sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ and lower detection rates at $T{=}11$; longer generation chains ($T{\geq}20$) could improve both methods' power.
Our method recommendation (permutation Granger) is robust at $T{=}10$; threshold onset could become viable at $T{\geq}20$ with additional degrees of freedom.
We omit transfer entropy, a standard nonlinear Granger alternative, because kernel density estimation requires substantially longer time series (typically $T{\geq}100$) than our 10-generation design permits, yielding negligible statistical power at $T{=}10$.
Classical critical slowing down (CSD) indicators---rising autocorrelation (AC1) and variance---similarly require substantially longer time series ($T{\geq}50$--$100$; \citealt{dakos2012methods}) for reliable detection; our $T{=}11$ sequences are insufficient to test whether CSD signatures accompany the onset of causal detectability, which we leave to future work with extended generation protocols.
Longer generation chains would improve statistical power but impose substantial computational cost.

\paragraph{Bivariate Granger $\neq$ causality.}
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders.
An unobserved process (such as a latent shift in the training data distribution) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations.
Our multi-method consensus framework mitigates but does not eliminate this limitation; multivariate VAR models would be required to test for confounders directly.

\paragraph{Regime boundary uncertainty.}
The onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$ has been refined by probing at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$ (all 0/8), narrowing the transition to a ${\leq}0.05$-wide interval; a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (FDR $p{=}0.053$) but does not reach aggregate detection.
Sigmoid regression (\S\ref{sec:regime}) characterizes this boundary as near-discontinuous ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, steepness $k{\geq}200$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), but whether this sharpness is preserved at larger model scales or different data domains remains open.
Three-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.75$ on WikiText confirms directional asymmetry (20/24 forward, 0/24 reverse) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), leaving the exact boundary position uncertain.
Directional asymmetry itself is domain-dependent: C4 exhibits near-symmetric bidirectional coupling at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (PermG reverse 7/8; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), and whether this pattern generalizes to other domains or contamination levels is untested.
The canary blind spot observed at $\alpha{=}0.10$ (diversity collapsed but canary silent) rests on a single seed; multi-seed confirmation is needed to establish whether this dissociation is robust.

\paragraph{Intervention scope.}
Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}) validate canary-based predictive cessation across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, but only at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (full synthetic replacement).
Whether the 15\% entropy threshold remains effective under partial contamination or accumulate-mode training is untested; the $\alpha{=}0.60$ trigger observation (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) remains without intervention validation.

\paragraph{Replace-only protocol.}
Our experiments use replace-only data accumulation; accumulate-mode training~\cite{dey2024breaking,kazdan2025collapse} may exhibit qualitatively different canary dynamics or eliminate the need for canary monitoring entirely~\cite{falahati2026curated}.

\paragraph{Scope limited to diversity metrics.}
Our canary claims are scoped to distinct-$n$ diversity metrics~\cite{li2016diversity}, not to model collapse broadly~\cite{schaeffer2025position}, as the perplexity channel proved spurious after differencing.
This scoping is theoretically motivated by the calibration-diversity tradeoff~\cite{cao2025entropycal}, but means our findings may not generalize to other collapse manifestations (e.g., factual degradation, reasoning capability loss).

file.content:
meta:
  title: "Method Matters: Pitfalls and a Multi-Method Consensus Framework for Lead-Lag Analysis in Iterative Training Collapse"
  venue: EMNLP 2026
  track: main
  deadline: "2026-06-15 (estimated, ARR submission)"
  format: "ACL/EMNLP two-column, 8 pages + unlimited references/appendix"
  template: "acl2023"
  template_note: "D043: 投稿目标从 AAAI 2027 变更为 EMNLP 2026 main track。使用 ACL 2023 模板（acl2023.sty），EMNLP 2026 沿用 ACL 格式"
  word_budget_total: 7200
  citation_budget: 40-45
  status: approved

paper_outline:
  - section: abstract
    word_budget: 200
    dependencies: [method, experiments, introduction]
    key_points:
      - "Problem: lead-lag analysis in model collapse lacks methodological rigor"
      - "Gap: method choice can flip conclusions; no systematic sensitivity analysis exists"
      - "Approach: 3 pitfalls + multi-method consensus framework with FPR/FNR calibration"
      - "Results: naive correlation 100% sig → differenced Granger 25%; consensus framework achieves FPR=0/FNR=0 on reference extremes"
      - "Case study: token entropy Granger-causes diversity collapse at α≥0.75 with 1-gen lead"

  - section: introduction
    word_budget: 1100
    dependencies: []
    key_points:
      - "Model collapse 文献日益关注 lead-lag 分析（Du et al., SIGMA, DCES），但方法论基础薄弱"
      - "Gap: 无差分检验、无多方法交叉验证、无 FDR 校正、无 regime-dependent 分析"
      - "Our approach: systematic case study exposing 3 pitfalls + consensus framework"
      - "Headline: naive 100% sig → differenced 25%; same test flips across α regimes"
      - "Contribution statement (D042): diagnostic + prescriptive framework with empirically calibrated thresholds"
    contributions:
      - "C1: 系统性暴露 lead-lag 分析中三个方法论陷阱（method sensitivity, spurious regression, regime dependence）"
      - "C2: 多方法共识框架 + empirically calibrated thresholds，FPR=0/FNR=0 on reference extremes"
      - "C3: 应用框架识别 token entropy 为 diversity collapse 的 1-gen-ahead canary（α≥0.75），附分层实用指南"

  - section: related_work
    word_budget: 900
    dependencies: [introduction]
    key_points:
      - "Model collapse foundations: Shumailov et al. 2024, Alemohammad et al. 2024, Dohmatob et al. 2024/2025"
      - "Canary/monitoring: chen2025scales (ECE先于accuracy), SIGMA (spectral), Kalinowski (topology), Gambetta (surplexity)"
      - "Data mixing theory: Kazdan et al. 2025, Dey et al. 2024, Fu et al. 2025, He et al. 2025 golden ratio"
      - "Early warning signals: Scheffer et al. 2009/2012 (tipping points), Boettiger & Hastings 2012 (detection limits)"
      - "与 Du et al. 4 点显式区分：多指标/多方法/regime mapping/方法敏感性"
    literature_clusters:
      - name: core_collapse
        must_cite: [shumailov2024curse, alemohammad2024mad, dohmatob2024tale, dohmatob2025strong, truong2025entropy]
        target_count: 6
      - name: canary_monitoring
        must_cite: [chen2025scales, sigma2026spectral, kalinowski2026topology]
        target_count: 5
      - name: data_mixing
        must_cite: [kazdan2025collapse, dey2024breaking, fu2025selfconsuming]
        target_count: 4
      - name: early_warning_tipping
        must_cite: [scheffer2009early, scheffer2012anticipating, boettiger2012limits]
        target_count: 3
      - name: methodology_granger
        must_cite: [shojaie2022granger]
        target_count: 2
      - name: diversity_metrics
        must_cite: [li2016diversity, guo2024linguistic]
        target_count: 2

  - section: background
    word_budget: 500
    dependencies: []
    key_points:
      - "Iterative training loop 形式化定义：M_t, D_synth, α mixing ratio"
      - "Metric families: canary (token_entropy, ECE) vs downstream (distinct_1/2, perplexity)"
      - "Lead-lag testing problem: 给定两条时间序列，判定是否存在 temporal precedence"
      - "5 种方法简述：naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, threshold onset, permutation Granger, Toda-Yamamoto"

  - section: method
    word_budget: 1300
    dependencies: [background]
    subsections:
      - name: "Methodological Pitfalls in Lead-Lag Analysis"
        word_budget: 400
        key_points:
          - "Pitfall 1 — Method sensitivity: naive Pearson 100% sig vs permutation Granger 25% (16/16 → 6/16)"
          - "Pitfall 2 — Spurious regression: canary→perplexity 差分后 0/8 SIG (F≈0, p=0.99)，diversity 通道不变"
          - "Pitfall 3 — Regime dependence: 同一检验 α=1.0 24/24 FDR-sig → α≤0.50 0/8"
      - name: "Multi-Method Consensus Framework"
        word_budget: 500
        key_points:
          - "Definition: pair (X,Y) classified ROBUST iff ≥K/M methods judge significant AND ≥S/N seeds replicate"
          - "Sequential filtering pipeline: naive → differencing → Granger+FDR → multi-seed"
          - "Default: K=4/5, S=3/4 (empirically calibrated)"
      - name: "Empirical Calibration"
        word_budget: 300
        key_points:
          - "FPR from α=0.0 null control (no synthetic data)"
          - "FNR from α=1.0 (4 seeds, 6 ground-truth robust pairs)"
          - "K=4/5 S=3/4 achieves FPR=0 FNR=0 on reference extremes"
          - "D041 约束: FNR 独立验证 via D017 differencing"
          - "Discussion 声明: calibration limited to current setup"

  - section: experiments
    word_budget: 2100
    dependencies: [method]
    subsections:
      - name: "Experimental Setup"
        word_budget: 300
        key_points:
          - "Pythia-410M, WikiText-103 5K subset, 10 generations, 5000 steps/gen"
          - "α ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0}, seeds {42,43,44,45}"
          - "Metrics: token_entropy, ECE (next-token), distinct_1/2/3, perplexity"
          - "Statistical: BH FDR q=0.05, 5000 permutations"
      - name: "Method Sensitivity Analysis (Claim 3)"
        word_budget: 500
        key_points:
          - "5-method ablation: naive→differenced→threshold→permG→TY sig rates"
          - "2×2 差分对比: diversity channel (12/12→12/12) vs perplexity channel (8/8→0/8)"
          - "d_max sensitivity: 0%↔94% spurious rate swing"
          - "Cohen κ=0.185 (poor inter-method agreement)"
          - "method × α interaction: naive 100% everywhere vs permG dose-response"
          - "Ref to Fig 2"
      - name: "Regime-Dependent Detectability (Claim 2)"
        word_budget: 400
        key_points:
          - "5-point regime map: Granger FDR sig rate vs α"
          - "Detectability boundary at α≈0.50-0.75"
          - "Raw drift magnitude dose-response (primary): distinct_1 -14%→-40%→-93%"
          - "Non-monotonic diversity decline at α=0.25 (single-seed caveat)"
          - "α=0.50 null = positive finding (synchronous collapse, no temporal lead)"
          - "Ref to Fig 1, Fig 3"
      - name: "Case Study: Canary Prediction (Claim 1)"
        word_budget: 400
        key_points:
          - "token_entropy Granger-causes distinct_1/2 at α≥0.75"
          - "α=1.0: 24/24 FDR-sig across 4 seeds, cross-corr lag=+1 (r>0.99, std=0.0)"
          - "α=0.75: 3/4 FDR-sig (single-seed, C001 caveat), entropy→d1 borderline p_fdr=0.054"
          - "ECE as conditional secondary canary (equivalent in 4/5 methods, TY Type II only)"
          - "Consensus framework application: 6/16 robust pairs survive full pipeline"
          - "Ref to Fig 4, Fig 5"
      - name: "Consensus Framework Validation"
        word_budget: 200
        key_points:
          - "FPR=0 at α=0.0 null control"
          - "FNR=0 on 6 reference robust pairs (independently validated by D017 differencing)"
          - "Comparison: naive FPR=100%, TY FNR=25%"
          - "Ref to Table 3"

  - section: discussion
    word_budget: 700
    dependencies: [experiments]
    key_points:
      - "Granger precedence ≠ true causality (Granger 1969); bivariate cannot exclude confounders"
      - "Calibration limited to current setup (Pythia-410M, WikiText-103); generalization needs independent validation"
      - "FPR/FNR dimension asymmetry (D041): FPR method-only, FNR method×seed joint"
      - "Phase 3 three-phase dynamics (if multi-seed confirmed): observation window sensitivity as Claim 3 evidence"
      - "Limitations: single architecture family, T=10 short series, no intervention experiment"
      - "Future work: multi-variate VAR, cross-architecture validation, online monitoring integration"

  - section: conclusion
    word_budget: 250
    dependencies: [discussion]
    key_points:
      - "Method choice matters: 3 pitfalls that can flip lead-lag conclusions"
      - "Consensus framework: actionable from exploratory to publication-grade"
      - "Practical takeaway: token entropy as 1-gen-ahead canary for diversity collapse at α≥0.75"

3	
4	When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
5	Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
6	As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
7	By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
8	This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
9	The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.
10	Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators, and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
11	
12	Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims has received little scrutiny.
13	Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends, is a question that existing analyses leave unresolved.
14	Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
15	In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
16	This makes the validity of existing canary claims an open question with direct consequences for practitioners who rely on such signals to trigger training interventions.
17	
18	We identify four specific deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
19	(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends, a well-documented hazard in analyses of co-trending time series~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
20	(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined; no multi-method cross-validation is conducted.
21	(3)~No false discovery rate (FDR) correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg) guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
22	(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
23	The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who report that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
24	Their analysis, however, covers a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and relies on visual comparisons without statistical tests.
25	The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating} provides theoretical motivation but has not been applied to training collapse with the rigor that such short, non-stationary series require.
26	
27	We address these gaps through a multiverse-style analysis~\cite{bell2022modeling,kapoor2024reforms} of canary prediction of diversity collapse, the progressive loss of lexical diversity (as measured by distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}) across training generations.
28	Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we apply five statistical methods to expose three methodological pitfalls (method sensitivity, spurious regression, and regime dependence) through the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT), a formal FPR-inverse-weighted consensus framework inspired by specification curve analysis~\cite{simonsohn2020specification}.
29	An extended eight-point regime map ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) reveals a canary blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, diversity has already collapsed measurably but canary metrics remain at null levels, which places a detection lower bound at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$.
30	Permutation Granger causality emerges as the only method with both zero null-control FPR and high sensitivity; applied to token entropy, it identifies a robust one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse, and early detection enables timely cessation of synthetic-data training, reducing peak perplexity by 58\% compared to reactive cessation at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
31	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B confirms that these findings transfer beyond the primary experimental platform.
32	Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics, not model collapse broadly.
33	To our knowledge, this constitutes the first multiverse-style analysis of lead-lag claims in model collapse: the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions that span the full spectrum from universal significance to complete null.
34	
35	Our contributions are:
36	\begin{enumerate}
37	    \item \textbf{Systematic multi-method evaluation framework} (\S\ref{sec:method}, \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
38	    We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the same data and expose three methodological pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\% (inter-method $\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 20/24 FDR-significant pairs at $\alpha{=}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.
39	    The Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) formalizes this comparison through FPR-inverse weighted consensus with null-calibrated $p$-values.
40	    Shapley-value decomposition (exact 32-coalition enumeration; Figure~\ref{fig:shapley}) identifies naive cross-correlation as the sole FPR driver (Shapley(FPR)${=}{+}0.348$) and permutation Granger as the strongest suppressor (Shapley(FPR)${=}{-}0.194$).
41	
42	    \item \textbf{Permutation Granger causality as the recommended detection method} (\S\ref{sec:case_study}, \S\ref{sec:generalization}).
43	    Among the five methods evaluated, permutation Granger causality (PermG) is the only one combining zero null-control FPR with high sensitivity.
44	    PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse: on WikiText-103, 24/24 forward-direction pairs are FDR-significant and 0/24 in the reverse direction at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 seeds $\times$ 6 metric pairs), confirmed across GPT-2-medium, OPT-1.3B, and four additional model families.
45	    Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 cases (86\%).
46	    At $\alpha{=}0.75$, three-seed replication yields 20/24 forward and 0/24 reverse.
47	    This claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$); the perplexity channel is spurious.
48	
49	    \item \textbf{Dose-response characterization revealing a detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
50	    A signal-times-resolution framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}) predicts non-monotonic detectability; PermG confirms a four-regime structure: 0/8 through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (blind), near-discontinuous onset at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, dual-seed), a synchronous dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (0--3/8), and reliable detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ (5--6/8 per seed, three seeds; 6/8 per seed at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).
51	    Sigmoid regression quantifies the onset as a detection phase transition ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), occurring despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the transition boundary.

53	
54	    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection and cessation} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).

60

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators, and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.

Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims has received little scrutiny.
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends, is a question that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
This makes the validity of existing canary claims an open question with direct consequences for practitioners who rely on such signals to trigger training interventions.

We identify four specific deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends, a well-documented hazard in analyses of co-trending time series~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined; no multi-method cross-validation is conducted.
(3)~No false discovery rate (FDR) correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg) guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who report that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, covers a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and relies on visual comparisons without statistical tests.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating} provides theoretical motivation but has not been applied to training collapse with the rigor that such short, non-stationary series require.

We address these gaps through a multiverse-style analysis~\cite{bell2022modeling,kapoor2024reforms} of canary prediction of diversity collapse, the progressive loss of lexical diversity (as measured by distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}) across training generations.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we apply five statistical methods to expose three methodological pitfalls (method sensitivity, spurious regression, and regime dependence) through the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT), a formal FPR-inverse-weighted consensus framework inspired by specification curve analysis~\cite{simonsohn2020specification}.
An extended eight-point regime map ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) reveals a canary blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, diversity has already collapsed measurably but canary metrics remain at null levels, which places a detection lower bound at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$.
Permutation Granger causality emerges as the only method with both zero null-control FPR and high sensitivity; applied to token entropy, it identifies a robust one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse, and early detection enables timely cessation of synthetic-data training, reducing peak perplexity by 58\% compared to reactive cessation at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B confirms that these findings transfer beyond the primary experimental platform.
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics, not model collapse broadly.
To our knowledge, this constitutes the first multiverse-style analysis of lead-lag claims in model collapse: the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions that span the full spectrum from universal significance to complete null.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Systematic multi-method evaluation framework} (\S\ref{sec:method}, \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
    We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the same data and expose three methodological pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\% (inter-method $\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 20/24 FDR-significant pairs at $\alpha{=}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.
    The Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) formalizes this comparison through FPR-inverse weighted consensus with null-calibrated $p$-values.
    Shapley-value decomposition (exact 32-coalition enumeration; Figure~\ref{fig:shapley}) identifies naive cross-correlation as the sole FPR driver (Shapley(FPR)${=}{+}0.348$) and permutation Granger as the strongest suppressor (Shapley(FPR)${=}{-}0.194$).

    \item \textbf{Permutation Granger causality as the recommended detection method} (\S\ref{sec:case_study}, \S\ref{sec:generalization}).
    Among the five methods evaluated, permutation Granger causality (PermG) is the only one combining zero null-control FPR with high sensitivity.
    PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse: on WikiText-103, 24/24 forward-direction pairs are FDR-significant and 0/24 in the reverse direction at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 seeds $\times$ 6 metric pairs), confirmed across GPT-2-medium, OPT-1.3B, and four additional model families.
    Cross-architecture validation across 14 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 12 cases (86\%).
    At $\alpha{=}0.75$, three-seed replication yields 20/24 forward and 0/24 reverse.
    This claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$); the perplexity channel is spurious.

    \item \textbf{Dose-response characterization revealing a detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    A signal-times-resolution framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}) predicts non-monotonic detectability; PermG confirms a four-regime structure: 0/8 through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (blind), near-discontinuous onset at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, dual-seed), a synchronous dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (0--3/8), and reliable detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ (5--6/8 per seed, three seeds; 6/8 per seed at $\alpha{=}1.0$, four seeds).
    Sigmoid regression quantifies the onset as a detection phase transition ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), occurring despite only 0.15 percentage points difference in cumulative contamination across the transition boundary.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed (distinct-1 drops 39.6\%) but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null condition (entropy drift $-5.3\%$ vs.\ null $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$, a gap of less than one percentage point).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection and cessation} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    As a practical demonstration, we compare predictive cessation (triggered when token entropy drops ${>}15\%$) against reactive cessation (triggered when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$).
    The entropy-based trigger fires one generation earlier, enabling cessation of synthetic-data training before irreversible damage: peak perplexity is reduced by 58\% (pooled estimate; bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%)\footnote{Bootstrap CI computed from two seed-precision pairs (s42 fp32, s43 bf16); the interval reflects observed variation rather than population-level uncertainty.} and convergence completes one generation faster (Generation~2 vs.\ Generation~3).
    At $\alpha{=}0.75$, entropy drops 31.6\% at generation~1, exceeding the 15\% threshold and confirming that the trigger generalizes beyond full synthetic replacement.
    Results are validated at $\alpha{=}1.0$ across two model scales: Pythia-410M (s42 fp32; s43 bf16, subject to precision effects discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}) and Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32), confirming that the trigger and recovery pattern is scale-independent.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}), cross-architecture generalization (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), and canary-based early intervention (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).

8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across six contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
9	Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
15	The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.10$ uses a single seed (42, preliminary).
16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
20	Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
21	We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24	
25	All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
26	Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
27	Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.

50	\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
51	\label{sec:method_sensitivity}
52	
53	We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
54	If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.
55	
56	\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
57	We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
58	The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{5/16} (31.3\%; moderate supplementary, \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
59	Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 37.5\%} among the primary methods: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
60	The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is at least \textbf{62.5\%} across the primary methods.
61	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.
62	
63	\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
64	A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
65	For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
66	For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
67	The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
68	Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.
69	
70	\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
71	Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
72	After correcting the statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$; however, the qualitative finding that this single hyperparameter can swing conclusions between near-universal significance and near-universal non-significance remains, consistent with known properties of the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical}.
73

81	\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
82	Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
83	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
84	Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation, which anchors the permissive extreme, and Toda--Yamamoto, which provides moderate supplementary signal) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
85	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
86	Direction checking (D111) itself constitutes a sensitivity dimension beyond the five statistical methods: restricting to forward-direction associations inverts naive cross-correlation's profile from uniformly high (${\approx}100\%$ undirected) to regime-dependent, revealing that much of its apparent signal was reverse-directional.
87	At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control), naive cross-correlation still finds \textbf{75\%} (6/8) of forward-direction pairs significant---lower than the undirected 100\%, but still a substantial FPR.
88	Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\%, achieving perfect null-control specificity.
89	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), permutation Granger finds 75\% (6/8), while naive finds 37.5\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}; Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
90	
91	\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
92	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that direction checking reshapes the method hierarchy across contamination levels.
93	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, naive cross-correlation drops to 12.5\% while permutation Granger remains at 0\%, narrowing the gap visible in undirected analysis.
94	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, naive rises to 87.5\% while permutation Granger reaches 75\%; both methods detect, but naive's persistent 75\% null-control FPR means its high-$\alpha$ detections cannot be distinguished from false positives without the consensus framework.
95	This regime-dependent reversal, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.
96	
97	\paragraph{Why permutation Granger succeeds.}
98	The systematic comparison identifies PermG as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across all regimes where signal exists ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$).
99	Three properties explain this outcome.
100	First, the nonparametric permutation procedure inherently controls FPR by constructing the null distribution from the observed data rather than from distributional assumptions, making it robust to the non-stationarity that inflates false positives in correlation-based methods.
101	Second, Granger tests are directional by construction: they test whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history, naturally filtering the reverse-directional associations that inflate naive cross-correlation's FPR.
102	Third, PermG does not require threshold calibration or augmentation order selection, avoiding the hyperparameter sensitivity observed in Toda--Yamamoto (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}) and the power limitations that reduce threshold onset to near-zero detection under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}).
103	By contrast, differenced cross-correlation retains 100\% FDR significance in both forward \emph{and} reverse directions at $\alpha{=}0.75$, failing to distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics; and Toda--Yamamoto, while achieving moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
104	These complementary failures, exposed through the MMCT evaluation framework, converge on a single recommendation: for short iterative training series ($T{\leq}20$), permutation Granger causality should be the primary detection method.

132	\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
133	\label{sec:regime}
134	
135	Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
136	We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.
137	
138	\paragraph{Raw drift.}
139	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
140	Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets).
141	A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ reveals a steep diversity cliff: distinct-1 drops by 39.6\%, nearly matching the 3-seed mean at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$); distinct-2 shows a comparable jump ($-56.4\%$ vs.\ $-56.4{\pm}0.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$).
142	Token entropy at $\alpha{=}0.10$, however, differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$), constituting a canary blind spot in which diversity has already collapsed but no canary metric responds.
143	At higher contamination, distinct-1 decline continues: $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
144	The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

156	\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
157	Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
158	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/8 pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (including $\alpha{=}0.25$ where a faint single-pair signal appears at FDR $p{=}0.053$ but aggregate detection remains null, and $\alpha{=}0.35$/$0.40$/$0.45$ which confirm PermG fwd${=}$0/8), \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent), \textbf{3/8} and \textbf{0/8} at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (s42 and s43 respectively; dual-seed confirmed non-monotonic dip), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
159	At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 20/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
160	Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
161	Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
162	Permutation Granger forward significance is the primary detection indicator (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}): it reaches 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, dips to 3/8 at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (synchronous collapse zone; see below), and recovers to 5--6/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
163	The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$: finer-grained probing at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$ yields PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at all three levels, extending the blind spot through $\alpha{=}0.45$.
164	A faint signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (best-pair FDR $p{=}0.053$) but does not translate to aggregate detection; reliable detection begins at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, 2~seeds).
165	This near-discontinuous onset is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
166	Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
167	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach significance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

189	\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
190	Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
191	The transition from undetectable to reliably detectable occurs between $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: finer-grained probing confirms PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$, while $\alpha{=}0.50$ achieves 6/8 (2~seeds).
192	A faint single-pair signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (entropy$\to$distinct-1: raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), but all aggregate indicators remain null through $\alpha{=}0.45$, placing the onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$.
193	At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
194	Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.
195	
196	\paragraph{Quantifying the onset boundary.}
197	Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies the sharp onset observed above.
198	Fitting $P(\alpha) = 1/(1 + \exp(-k(\alpha - \alpha_c)))$ to the PermG forward detection rate yields a critical threshold $\alpha_c = 0.476$ with steepness $k \geq 200$ and transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
199	The sigmoid model explains 96.9\% of variance ($R^2 = 0.969$), substantially outperforming a power-law alternative ($R^2 = 0.808$; $\Delta\text{AIC} = 18.2$), confirming that the onset is near-discontinuous rather than gradual.
200	This transition is striking because effective contamination barely changes across the boundary: after 10 generations of iterative training, both $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$ drive the cumulative synthetic fraction above 99\% ($C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$: $99.75\%$ vs.\ $99.90\%$)---a difference of 0.15 percentage points---yet causal detectability jumps from 0/8 to 6/8.
201	We term this a \emph{detection phase transition}: causal coupling emerges abruptly at a critical contamination threshold ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$) rather than scaling smoothly with contamination dose.
202	Within the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}), $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ localizes the point at which signal strength $S(\alpha)$ first crosses the detection floor, while the high steepness ($k \geq 200$) indicates that temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ remains large at onset---the entropy--diversity lag has not yet begun to compress.
203	Cross-architecture comparison reveals no monotonic relationship between model scale and onset sensitivity (Qwen-0.8B $\approx$ Pythia-6.9B $>$ Pythia-410M $>$ Pythia-1.4B $>$ SmolLM3-3B), suggesting that architecture and pre-training data exert stronger influence than parameter count on detection onset.
